intro: The largest bristlecone pine ever measured, the Patriarch, stands in Patriarch Grove, not the more famous Schulman Grove where Methuselah, at 4,858 years the oldest tree species record-holder, grows unmarked to protect it. Its fame is bulk rather than age. It is broader and less twisted than the wind-carved bristlecones around it, on bare rock at nearly 3,440 metres in California's White Mountains, and nobody has published its age, height or girth. Near Schulman Grove a reader photographed a second, all ribbons of bare orange wood beside a rocky trail.
meta_description: The Patriarch Tree is the largest bristlecone pine known, in Patriarch Grove, California's White Mountains. Nobody has published its age.
question_meta: The Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest's best-known mapped tree is the Patriarch, the largest bristlecone pine known, in Patriarch Grove, not Schulman Grove.
question_answer: The Patriarch Tree, in Patriarch Grove, about 13 miles north of the more visited Schulman Grove. It is the largest bristlecone pine known by trunk volume, though a broader and comparatively untwisted trunk rather than a taller or older one: Methuselah, the species' age record-holder at 4,858 years, grows in Schulman Grove and is a different tree entirely. Nobody has published the Patriarch's age, height or girth. A second tree on this page, a twisted bristlecone beside a trail near Schulman Grove, came from a reader.
question_context:
The Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest sits in the White Mountains of eastern California, inside Inyo National Forest, and holds the oldest confirmed trees on Earth, some past 4,800 years. This page maps two of them. The Patriarch stands in Patriarch Grove, at about 3,440 metres, roughly 13 miles by a rough but maintained dirt road north of the Schulman Grove visitor centre, where the modest entry fee is paid. It is almost the first tree on the Timberline Ancients Trail from the grove's car park.

Its fame is size rather than age. Most bristlecones nearby are twisted into knots and ribbons of bare wood by the wind and cold at this elevation; the Patriarch is broader and comparatively straightforward, the bulkiest bristlecone anywhere by trunk volume. Methuselah, the oldest dated tree of any species at 4,858 years, grows in the Schulman Grove area, a different tree in a different grove, its exact location deliberately withheld to protect it. Nobody has published a height, girth or age for the Patriarch. The second, a twisted bristlecone beside a rocky trail near the Schulman Grove visitor centre, came from a reader; its age is unknown. The forest is open mid-May through November.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest?
faq.a: Neither tree mapped here has a published age. The forest's oldest tree of any kind is Methuselah, dated at 4,858 years, in the nearby but separate Schulman Grove; its exact location is withheld to protect it, so it is not one we can map.

faq.q: Why is it called the Patriarch if it isn't the oldest?
faq.a: Its fame is size, not age. It is the largest known bristlecone pine by trunk volume, broader and less wind-twisted than the trees around it, in a landscape where most bristlecones look nothing like it.
There is a modest entry fee, $3 per person or $6 per car maximum, paid at the Schulman Grove visitor centre gate; children under 18 are free.

By car via White Mountain Road from US-395 near Big Pine, California. From the Schulman Grove visitor centre, a rough but maintained dirt road (a spare tyre is recommended) runs about 13 miles north to Patriarch Grove, where the tree is almost the first stop on the Timberline Ancients Trail. The forest is generally open mid-May through November.

trees.story:
The largest bristlecone pine in the world does not look the part. Most of the ancient bristlecones around it are twisted into knots and ribbons of bare wood; the Patriarch is broader and comparatively straightforward, a heavy trunk of a tree in a landscape that seems to have given up on trees.

It stands in the Patriarch Grove, at about 3,440 metres in California's White Mountains, on ground that is mostly bare rock. This is the species that holds the record for longevity. Methuselah, down in the Schulman Grove area, has been dated at 4,858 years. The Patriarch is a different tree in a different grove, and its fame is size, not age. Both sources we used call it the largest bristlecone by trunk volume, and neither gives a number for its height, its girth or its age.

Methuselah's figure is not the Patriarch's, and nobody we can find has published how old the Patriarch is. If you know of a core or a count, tell us.

Getting there is part of it. From the Schulman Grove visitor centre, where the modest entry fee is paid, a rough but maintained dirt road runs about 21 kilometres north; take a spare tyre. The tree is almost the first thing on the Timberline Ancients Trail from the grove's car park. The forest is generally open from mid-May through November, weather permitting.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad, comparatively untwisted trunk, the bulkiest of the bristlecones around it. It stands almost at the start of the Timberline Ancients Trail in Patriarch Grove, not Schulman Grove.

trees.name: The Twisted Bristlecone by the Rocky Trail

location.address: Trail below Schulman Grove, Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest, Inyo National Forest, White Mountains, California

trees.how_to_recognise: Right beside a rocky trail: two stems of bare, twisted wood in ribbons of orange and cream, with green bottle-brush branches only at the top, and roots snaking over broken white rock.
trees.access: On a public trail in the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest; there is an entry fee at the Schulman Grove visitor centre, and the forest is generally open mid-May through November.
trees.story:
A reader walking the trails of the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest in August sent us this pine, photographed from the rocky path at its foot, less than a kilometre from the Schulman Grove visitor centre in California's White Mountains.

It looks the way people picture the oldest trees on Earth. Most of what you see is bare wood, stripped of bark and polished by wind, ice and blown grit into twisting ribbons of orange, cream and brown. Only a few strips of living bark still climb the stems to feed the green bottle-brush branches at the top. That is how bristlecones last so long: as the years go on they let most of themselves die back and keep a narrow lifeline alive. Below, the roots grip the broken white rock as if they had poured over it.

We do not know its age. Bristlecones in this forest run to thousands of years, and the oldest are deliberately left unmarked to protect them, so this page claims no record for this one and does not try to rank it. If you know more about it, tell us here.

Walk slowly along the path and look up at it against the deep blue of the mountain sky.
